# Conflict Matrix Stairs Guards Elevators


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the task in one sentence: what concept is being identified, compared, sequenced, or applied? Then anchor your answer to the article's stated scope and avoid importing details from a different topic.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **Conflict Matrix Stairs Guards Elevators** as enough to answer. For exam practice, first identify the exact concept being asked, then choose the option that matches that concept.
## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Apply the conflict-resolution hierarchy when PD 1096, BP 344, and other codes impose conflicting dimensional requirements on stairs, guards, and elevators; identify which code governs for each specific element (landing depth, handrail height, guard spacing, elevator cab size); and apply the strictest requirement principle consistently.
---

## REAL-WORLD HOOK

You are reviewing permit drawings for a mid-rise office building. The structural engineer has dimensioned the main stair at 1,200 mm clear width with a single handrail at 850 mm. The architect is citing PD 1096. The building official stamps it. Then BP 344 applies — and suddenly the stair needs to be 1,500 mm wide with *dual* handrails at 700 mm *and* 900 mm. The drawings go back. The slab is already poured.

This is not a theoretical problem. In the LEA, the examiner will hand you exactly this conflict and ask: *which law governs?* This module gives you the answer — every time.

---

## THE GOVERNING PRINCIPLE — KNOW THIS COLD

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="pd1096", section="Rule XII - Stairs and Guards"
- Text: When BP 344 and PD 1096 conflict, the MORE RESTRICTIVE (more accessibility-protective) provision governs.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]
>
> BP 344 is a special law protecting the rights of PWDs. PD 1096 is a general building regulation. Under the principle of *lex specialis derogat legi generali*, the special law prevails on matters of accessibility.
>
[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0002 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="bp344", section="Section 10 - Elevators"
- Text: Exception: Where PD 1096 sets a MORE restrictive dimension that also serves accessibility (e.g., greater guard height), the higher standard of both laws applies simultaneously.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Warn" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: ⚠️ Common Exam Trap: When PD 1096 and BP 344 both specify dimensions for the same element, do NOT simply average them. The stricter (more protective) standard always governs. Exception: if PD 1096 has a MORE restrictive dimension that also aids accessibility (e.g., higher guardrails), apply the higher of both standards.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="ExamTip" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: LEA Strategy: Draw a small T-chart on scratch paper. Left column = PD 1096 dimension. Right column = BP 344 dimension. Circle the stricter value. That is your answer. For stairs: PD 1096 allows 1,100 mm width; BP 344 requires 1,500 mm for accessible means of egress.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

## CORE MNEMONIC: **"DUAL GRIP — 700 PLUS 900"**

For BP 344 stairs and ramps, remember:
- **D**ual handrails — always two
- **G**rip diameter — 30–40 mm
- **7** — 700 mm lower rail (seated eye level)
- **9** — 900 mm upper rail (standard ambulatory height)
- **3** — 300 mm horizontal extension at top and bottom
- **5-0** — 50 mm clearance from wall to grip surface

*PD 1096 uses ONE rail in the 800–900 mm band. The exam will try to make you confuse these.*

---

## THE MASTER CONFLICT MATRIX TABLE

| Element | **BP 344 (2024 IRR)** | **PD 1096** | **Governing Rule** | **Exam Trap** |
|---------|----------------------|------------|-------------------|---------------|
| **Stair handrail — quantity** | **2 rails** (dual height) | 1 required (both sides if >3,000 mm wide) | **BP 344** governs: always dual | Exam may show 1 rail at 900 mm citing PD 1096 — **non-compliant** under BP 344 |
| **Stair handrail — lower height** | **700 mm** above nosing | Not specified (no lower rail) | **BP 344** adds lower rail at 700 mm | Confusing 700 mm (BP 344 lower) with PD 1096's 800 mm minimum |
| **Stair handrail — upper height** | **900 mm** above nosing | **800–900 mm** above nosing | Overlap: 900 mm satisfies both | PD 1096 allows 800 mm; BP 344 requires exactly 900 mm for upper rail |
| **Stair handrail — extensions** | **300 mm** horizontal at top + bottom | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Extensions are frequently omitted in drawings and tested on exam |
| **Handrail grip diameter** | **30–40 mm** | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Pipes >40 mm or <30 mm are non-compliant under BP 344 |
| **Clearance from wall** | **50 mm** min | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Flush-to-wall rails are non-compliant under BP 344 |
| **Handrail terminal at landing** | Bent at **150 mm radius** to newel | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Sharp-cut ends are non-compliant; safety hazard for cane users |
| **Handrail continuity at landings** | Continuous around landings **< 2,100 mm** | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Interrupted rail at landing = non-compliant if landing < 2,100 mm |
| **Intermediate handrail** | Both sides of all accessible stairs | Required if stair > **3,000 mm** wide (PD 1096) | **Both**: dual rail (BP 344) + intermediate if >3,000 mm (PD 1096) | Exam may conflate "intermediate" with "dual" |
| **Guard (balustrade) height** | **1,100 mm** where drop > 750 mm | **1,100 mm** where drop > 750 mm | **Same** — no conflict | Exact match; memorize as 1,100 mm = universal |
| **Stair clear width — accessible** | **1,500 mm** | 1,100 mm typical (occupancy varies) | **BP 344** governs for accessible routes | BP 344 standard nearly doubles typical NBC stair width |
| **Stair riser — max** | **150 mm** | 200 mm typical (varies) | **BP 344** governs: more restrictive | Many existing buildings have 175–200 mm risers — non-compliant for accessible routes |
| **Stair tread — min** | **300 mm** | 250 mm typical (varies) | **BP 344** governs: more restrictive | Exam may show 260 mm tread citing PD 1096 — acceptable under NBC, not under BP 344 |
| **Stair headroom — min** | Not separately specified in BP 344 | **2,000 mm** clear | **PD 1096** governs | BP 344 defers to NBC on headroom |
| **Landing — max vertical interval** | **3 m** (landing at every 3 m of vertical rise) | **3,600 mm** | **BP 344** governs: more restrictive (3,000 mm vs 3,600 mm) | **Major exam trap**: 3 m (BP 344) vs 3.6 m (PD 1096) |
| **Landing — min depth** | **1,500 mm** | Equal to stair width, max **1,200 mm** for straight | **BP 344** governs: 1,500 mm > 1,200 mm | BP 344 landing is deeper than PD 1096 max — can cause coordination issues |
| **Clear space before/after stair** | **1,200 mm** clear approach | Not specified separately | **BP 344** governs | The 1,200 mm approach zone is distinct from the landing |
| **Stair nosing** | Slip-resistant, **30% luminance contrast** | Slip-resistant (no contrast spec) | **BP 344** governs on contrast | PD 1096 only says slip-resistant; BP 344 adds visual contrast requirement |
| **Raised edge (stair sides)** | **100 mm** min curb on both sides | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Protects cane users; often missing from drawings |
| **Elevator car — buildings** | Min **1,200 × 1,400 mm**, door **900 mm** | Not specifically addressed | **BP 344** governs | Depth (1,400 mm) allows full wheelchair entry; smaller cabs are non-compliant |
| **Elevator car — transport facilities** | Min **1,500 × 1,400 mm**, door **900 mm** | Not addressed | **BP 344** governs: larger for transport | Building vs. transport distinction is a tested trap |
| **Elevator lobby** | **1,800 × 1,800 mm** | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Same 1,800 × 1,800 mm rule as other fixtures |
| **Elevator handrails** | **900 mm** on **3 walls** inside car | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Must be on 3 walls, not just 1 — exam tests completeness |
| **Elevator COP height** | **900 mm** AFF | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | COP = Car Operating Panel |
| **Elevator Braille on jambs** | **1,200 mm** AFF | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Braille floor numbers on outside door jambs |
| **Area of Refuge size** | **900 × 1,200 mm** per wheelchair user | Not specified in NBC | **BP 344** governs | Required at each stair landing serving as egress for PWDs |
| **Area of Refuge comms** | **700–900 mm** AFF | Not specified | **BP 344** governs | Emergency communication within reach range |

---

## CRITICAL CONFLICTS DECODED

### Conflict 1: The Handrail Height Battle (Most Tested)

```
PD 1096 STAIRCASE:
            ───────────  ← 800–900 mm above nosing (ONE rail, any height in this band)
           /
          /
         /

BP 344 STAIRCASE:
            ───────────  ← 900 mm above nosing (UPPER rail)
           /
          /
    ──────  ← 700 mm above nosing (LOWER rail)
         /

If a building is subject to BP 344 (i.e., public or private used by public):
→ BOTH rails required at EXACTLY 700 mm and 900 mm
→ PD 1096 allows 850 mm as sole handrail; BP 344 does NOT accept this
```

**The trap question:** *"A staircase has one handrail at 850 mm above the nosing. The building official approved it under PD 1096. Is it accessible?"*

**Answer:** **No.** BP 344 requires dual handrails at 700 mm AND 900 mm. A single rail at 850 mm — while compliant with PD 1096 — fails BP 344.

---

### Conflict 2: Landing Interval — 3 m vs. 3.6 m

| Law | Max vertical rise before landing |
|-----|----------------------------------|
| **BP 344** | **3,000 mm (3 m)** |
| **PD 1096** | **3,600 mm (3.6 m)** |
| **Governing** | **BP 344 — 3 m** |

A staircase in a public building may have been designed under PD 1096 with a landing at 3,500 mm vertical rise. This is **non-compliant** with BP 344. The more restrictive 3 m interval governs.

---

### Conflict 3: Landing Depth — Apparently Contradictory

| Law | Landing depth |
|-----|--------------|
| **BP 344** | Min **1,500 mm** |
| **PD 1096** | Equal to stair width, **max 1,200 mm** for straight stairs |
| **Governing** | **BP 344 — 1,500 mm** |

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="Note" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: PD 1096's "max 1,200 mm" is a ceiling for straight stairs (to prevent oversized landings that waste space). BP 344's "min 1,500 mm" is a floor for accessibility. Since a larger landing is more accessible, BP 344's 1,500 mm requirement governs — even though it exceeds PD 1096's stated maximum for standard stairs. The accessibility requirement takes precedence.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

### Conflict 4: Stair Clear Width

| Law | Minimum clear width |
|-----|-------------------|
| **BP 344** | **1,500 mm** (accessible staircases) |
| **PD 1096** | ~1,100 mm typical (varies by occupancy and floor area) |
| **Governing** | **BP 344 — 1,500 mm** for any stair on an accessible route |

---

### Conflict 5: Guards — The Non-Conflict

| Law | Guard height |
|-----|------------|
| **BP 344** | **1,100 mm** where drop > 750 mm |
| **PD 1096** | **1,100 mm** where drop > 750 mm |
| **Result** | **Perfect agreement.** |

> This is the one area of zero conflict. Both laws agree: **1,100 mm guards where drop exceeds 750 mm**. Examiners sometimes present this as a trap asking "which law governs?" — the answer is: **both specify 1,100 mm; no conflict exists**.

---

## ELEVATOR SPECIFICATIONS — DEEP DIVE

### Legal Basis: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Section 5.6 (Transport Facilities) and General Provisions

### Building Elevator vs. Transport Facility Elevator

| Feature | Standard Building Elevator | Transport Facility Elevator |
|---------|---------------------------|---------------------------|
| **Min car width** | 1,200 mm | **1,500 mm** |
| **Min car depth** | 1,400 mm | 1,400 mm |
| **Door clear width** | **900 mm** | **900 mm** |
| **Lobby clear space** | **1,800 × 1,800 mm** | **1,800 × 1,800 mm** |
| **Handrails inside** | 900 mm on **3 walls** | 900 mm on **3 walls** |
| **COP height** | **900 mm** AFF | **900 mm** AFF |
| **Braille on jambs** | **1,200 mm** AFF | **1,200 mm** AFF |
| **Rationale** | Wheelchair turnaround | Wider for transit crowds + mobility aids |

### Elevator Interior Spatial Sketch

```
BUILDING ELEVATOR (min):
 ┌──────────────┐
 │  1,200 mm    │  ← Width
 │              │
 │   1,400 mm   │  ← Depth
 │   (depth)    │
 │   HANDRAIL   │  ← 900 mm high, on 3 walls
 └──────────────┘
      900 mm door

TRANSPORT FACILITY ELEVATOR (min):
 ┌────────────────┐
 │   1,500 mm     │  ← Width (wider)
 │                │
 │   1,400 mm     │  ← Same depth
 │   (depth)      │
 └────────────────┘
       900 mm door
```

---

## > TRAP LEART #1 — Upper Handrail: 900 mm or 800–900 mm?

**PD 1096** says 800–900 mm (a range). **BP 344** says 900 mm (a fixed value). If asked what height an accessible stair upper handrail must be, the answer is **900 mm exactly** (BP 344 governs on accessible routes).

A drawing showing 850 mm is PD 1096-compliant but **BP 344-non-compliant** for accessible routes.

---

## > TRAP LEART #2 — Extensions Beyond the Stair

**BP 344** requires **300 mm horizontal extensions** at top and bottom of each handrail run. PD 1096 is silent. These 300 mm extensions are a signature BP 344 requirement that appears regularly on the LEA. Both the upper (900 mm) and lower (700 mm) rails need extensions.

---

## > TRAP LEART #3 — "3 m" Not "3,000 mm" Confusion

The landing interval under BP 344 is commonly written as "3 m vertical rise." This is exactly 3,000 mm. PD 1096's 3,600 mm is exactly 3.6 m. Examiners write these as decimals, fractions, or mixed units. Convert everything to mm for comparison.

---

## > TRAP LEART #4 — Elevator Handrails on 3 Walls

A common wrong answer is handrails on 1 wall (the back wall) or 2 walls. BP 344 requires the inside of the elevator cab to have handrails at 900 mm on **three walls** — typically the back wall and both side walls. The door wall has no handrail (it's the door).

---

## > TRAP LEART #5 — Area of Refuge vs. Wheelchair Parking vs. Elevator Lobby

All three have different clear spaces:

| Element | Clear Space |
|---------|------------|
| Area of Refuge | **900 × 1,200 mm** |
| Assembly wheelchair space | **900 × 1,200 mm** |
| Elevator lobby | **1,800 × 1,800 mm** |
| ATM / Phone / Fountain clear | **1,800 × 1,800 mm** |

Don't mix 900 × 1,200 mm (refuge/wheelchair) with 1,800 × 1,800 mm (elevator lobby/fixture approach).

---

## > TRAP LEART #6 — Raised Edge on Stair Sides

BP 344 requires a **100 mm raised edge** (curb) on both sides of accessible staircases. This is distinct from the handrail. Its purpose is to prevent a white-cane or foot from slipping off the stair edge. PD 1096 does not specify this. It is tested as a "detail frequently omitted from drawings."

---

## > TRAP LEART #7 — Stair Clear Width 1,500 mm vs. Corridor Clear Width

BP 344 stair clear width is **1,500 mm**. Corridor clear width is typically **1,200–1,500 mm** depending on the section. Do not conflate stair width with corridor width. The 1,500 mm stair standard is for accessible staircases; some corridors may be 1,200 mm minimum.

---

## AREAS OF REFUGE — INTEGRATION WITH STAIRS

### Legal Basis: BP 344 (2024 IRR) Section 5

| Element | Specification |
|---------|--------------|
| **Clear footprint per wheelchair** | **900 × 1,200 mm** |
| **Location** | At stair landings used as evacuation refuge |
| **Emergency communications** | Required at **700–900 mm** AFF |
| **Illumination** | **200 lux** |
| **Identification** | On tactile/Braille evacuation plan |
| **Access** | Must not require passing through another wheelchair space |

> Areas of refuge are mandatory because elevators are typically shut down during fire emergencies. PWDs who cannot use stairs must have a safe, protected space to wait for rescue. The 900 × 1,200 mm footprint matches one wheelchair parking space.

---

## STAIR SPECIFICATION MASTER CHECKLIST (BP 344 Standard)

```
ACCESSIBLE STAIRCASE COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST
==========================================
[ ] Clear width ≥ 1,500 mm
[ ] Max riser: 150 mm
[ ] Min tread: 300 mm
[ ] Nosing: slip-resistant + 30% luminance contrast
[ ] Raised curb edge: 100 mm min, both sides
[ ] Handrail lower: 700 mm above nosing (both sides)
[ ] Handrail upper: 900 mm above nosing (both sides)
[ ] Grip diameter: 30–40 mm
[ ] Wall clearance: 50 mm min
[ ] Extensions: 300 mm horizontal at top and bottom
[ ] Terminal: bent at 150 mm radius to newel
[ ] Continuous around landings < 2,100 mm
[ ] Landing at every 3 m vertical rise
[ ] Landing depth ≥ 1,500 mm
[ ] Clear approach space 1,200 mm before/after stair
[ ] Area of Refuge at evacuation landings: 900 × 1,200 mm
[ ] Emergency comms: 700–900 mm AFF
```

---

## QUICK SUMMARY: BP 344 WINS LIST

*The following are all cases where BP 344 is stricter than PD 1096 and therefore governs:*

1. **Dual handrails** (BP 344) vs. single handrail (PD 1096)
2. **700 mm lower handrail** (BP 344) — no equivalent in PD 1096
3. **900 mm upper handrail** (BP 344) vs. 800–900 mm band (PD 1096)
4. **300 mm extensions** (BP 344) — not in PD 1096
5. **Landing interval: 3 m** (BP 344) vs. 3.6 m (PD 1096)
6. **Landing depth: 1,500 mm** (BP 344) vs. max 1,200 mm typical (PD 1096)
7. **Stair clear width: 1,500 mm** (BP 344) vs. ~1,100 mm typical (PD 1096)
8. **Max riser 150 mm** (BP 344) vs. 200 mm typical (PD 1096)
9. **Min tread 300 mm** (BP 344) vs. 250 mm typical (PD 1096)
10. **Nosing luminance contrast** (BP 344) — not in PD 1096
11. **Raised stair edge 100 mm** (BP 344) — not in PD 1096
12. **Elevator car dimensions** (BP 344) — not addressed in PD 1096

### Where they agree:
- **Guards: 1,100 mm where drop > 750 mm** — same in both

---

## ACTIVE RECALL DRILL

**Q1.** BP 344 requires dual handrails on stairs. At what two heights?
> **A1.** 700 mm (lower) and 900 mm (upper) above the nosing.

**Q2.** PD 1096 permits a single handrail at 850 mm on a stair. Is this acceptable for an accessible route?
[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="bp344"
- Text: A2. No. BP 344 governs and requires dual handrails at 700 mm and 900 mm.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Q3.** What is the maximum vertical rise between stair landings under BP 344?
> **A3.** 3 m (3,000 mm).

**Q4.** What is the maximum vertical rise between stair landings under PD 1096?
> **A4.** 3,600 mm (3.6 m).

**Q5.** Which governs when they conflict?
[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0007 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="bp344"
- Text: A5. BP 344 (the more restrictive, accessibility-protective standard).
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Q6.** What is the minimum landing depth under BP 344?
> **A6.** 1,500 mm.

**Q7.** What is the minimum clear width for an accessible staircase under BP 344?
> **A7.** 1,500 mm.

**Q8.** What are the minimum elevator car dimensions for a building (non-transport)?
> **A8.** 1,200 mm wide × 1,400 mm deep, with 900 mm door.

**Q9.** What are the minimum elevator car dimensions for a transport facility?
> **A9.** 1,500 mm wide × 1,400 mm deep, with 900 mm door.

**Q10.** On how many walls inside an elevator car must handrails be installed, and at what height?
> **A10.** Three walls (back + two sides), at 900 mm AFF.

**Q11.** Where must Braille floor indicators be placed on an elevator?
> **A11.** On the jambs at 1,200 mm AFF.

**Q12.** What is the area of refuge footprint required per wheelchair user?
> **A12.** 900 × 1,200 mm.

**Q13.** What is the minimum guard height where a drop exceeds 750 mm?
[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0008 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="bp344"
- Text: A13. 1,100 mm (same in both BP 344 and PD 1096).
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Q14.** What horizontal extension is required at the top and bottom of each accessible stair handrail?
> **A14.** 300 mm.

---

## 60-SECOND BLITZ QUIZ

*6 seconds each — go!*

1. BP 344 dual handrail heights → **700 mm + 900 mm**
2. PD 1096 handrail range → **800–900 mm**
3. Which governs on accessible stairs? → **BP 344**
4. BP 344 max landing interval → **3 m**
5. PD 1096 max landing interval → **3.6 m**
6. BP 344 min landing depth → **1,500 mm**
7. Min stair clear width (BP 344) → **1,500 mm**
8. Guard height (both laws) → **1,100 mm**
9. Building elevator min width → **1,200 mm**
10. Transport elevator min width → **1,500 mm**
11. Elevator handrails → **3 walls at 900 mm**
12. Handrail extension → **300 mm**

**12/12 = You are exam-ready on this topic.**

---

## PROTÉGÉ EFFECT CHALLENGE

You are the accessibility consultant reviewing final permit drawings for a 10-story government office building. The architect has:

1. Shown a main stair with one handrail at 870 mm, citing PD 1096.
2. Drawn landings at every 3,400 mm of vertical rise.
3. Dimensioned the stair at 1,100 mm clear width.
4. Shown a standard elevator at 1,100 mm × 1,300 mm.
5. Placed handrails only on the back wall of the elevator.

Without looking at your notes:

- **Identify every violation** with the specific BP 344 provision it fails.
- **Provide the corrected dimension** for each.
- **Explain to the architect** why "PD 1096 compliance does not equal BP 344 compliance" and why both laws must be satisfied simultaneously.

*This is the exact scenario you will face as a licensed architect working in the Philippines. Master it now.*

---

## Cross-Referencing

### Connection to BP 344 Accessible Washrooms
The 1,800 × 1,800 mm elevator lobby clear space matches the BP 344 requirement for accessible washroom turning space. This is not a coincidence — BP 344 uses this universal turning radius for all fixture approach clearances.

### Connection to Commercial Clearances
The 1,500 mm stair clear width under BP 344 matches the dining circulation path minimum. Both derive from the minimum space needed for a wheelchair user and an ambulatory person to pass.

### Connection to Widths & Slopes
The 1:15 maximum ramp slope and 1,800 mm landing dimensions in the ramp article coordinate with the stair landing requirements here. A ramp and stair sharing a landing in a vertical core must both satisfy BP 344 minimums — the largest dimension governs.

### Connection to PD 1096 Rule XII (Means of Egress)
PD 1096 governs exit stair capacity (number of exits, occupant load, travel distance). BP 344 overlays accessibility dimensions on top of these life-safety requirements. Neither law can be satisfied in isolation — a compliant building must meet both simultaneously.

# Accessible Seating in Assembly Areas


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the task in one sentence: what concept is being identified, compared, sequenced, or applied? Then anchor your answer to the article's stated scope and avoid importing details from a different topic.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **Accessible Seating in Assembly Areas** as enough to answer. For exam practice, first identify the exact concept being asked, then choose the option that matches that concept.
## Learning Goal
After reading this article, you should be able to:

Calculate the number and distribution of accessible wheelchair seating locations required in assembly areas under BP 344; apply sightline requirements (18° maximum vertical angle, companion seating); determine which row locations satisfy dispersion requirements; and identify when accessible seating must be provided on each tier or balcony level.
---

## REAL-WORLD HOOK

> You walk into a 750-seat cinema on opening night. The trailers begin. Somewhere in the back row, a person in a wheelchair cannot see the screen because the only "wheelchair area" is at the far left corner, blocked by the accessible route itself. Her companion stands awkwardly in the aisle. In front of her, another wheelchair user must pass through her space to reach his seat. The theater was built in 2005 under the old IRR. Now it's 2026. The new IRR is in force. **Would this theater pass inspection?** Almost certainly not — on at least four separate counts. This module tells you every one of them.

---

## CORE MNEMONIC FRAMEWORK

### **"DISC — WAH — 5P"**

| Letter | Stands For | What It Means |
|--------|-----------|---------------|
| **D** | **Dispersal** | Spaces spread throughout the seating bowl |
| **I** | **Independent Access** | No wheelchair space accessed through another |
| **S** | **Sightlines** | Unobstructed views; companion seats beside, not behind |
| **C** | **Circulation Separation** | Accessible route CANNOT overlap wheelchair spaces |
| **W** | **Width × Depth** | 900 mm × 1200 mm minimum footprint per space |
| **A** | **Adjoin Circulation** | Viewing areas must adjoin accessible circulation routes |
| **H** | **Handrails at 750 mm** | Front and sides of wheelchair positions |
| **5P** | **5% Priority Waiting** | 5% of waiting-area seats reserved for PWDs |

---

## LEGAL FOUNDATION

| Law / Instrument | Relevance |
|-----------------|-----------|
| **BP 344 (2024 IRR), Appendix D, Sec. 4** | Assembly seating accessibility standards |
| **BP 344 (2024 IRR), Appendix D, Sec. 18.2.b.iii** | 5% priority waiting seats |
| **BP 344 (2024 IRR), Appendix D, Sec. 3.3.a** | Companion seats in sports facilities |
| **RA 7277 (Magna Carta for PWDs)** | Right to equal access in public places |
| **RA 9442** | Anti-ridicule; enhanced privileges |
| **RA 10754** | 20% discount + VAT exemption for PWDs |
| **PD 1096 (NBC), Rule XII** | General stair/handrail minimums (conflict zone) |

## REASON FOR THE LAW

### Why 3% and Not a Flat Number?
Because **scale matters**. A 50-seat chapel needs far fewer WC spaces than a 10,000-seat arena. The old tiered table was an approximation; the 3% rule is proportional and eliminates the "cliff effect" (e.g., a 499-seat hall needed only 6 spaces, but a 501-seat hall needed 7).

### Why Can't an Accessible Route Overlap a Wheelchair Space? (Sec. 4.2)
Because when a wheelchair user occupies that space, a circulation route running through it would **trap or block them**. The space must be a safe haven, not a corridor.

### Why Can't You Access One WC Space Through Another? (Sec. 4.3)
Dignity and independence. If wheelchair user A must move to let wheelchair user B reach their space, **B's accessibility is contingent on A's cooperation** — which violates the principle of autonomous access enshrined in RA 7277.

### Why 750 mm Handrails at WC Positions? (Sec. 4.7)
Seated wheelchair users reach forward at approximately 750–800 mm. A 900 mm handrail (standard stair height) is **too high for lateral support** from a seated position. The 750 mm height aligns with the natural arm reach of a person seated in a wheelchair.

### Why 5% Priority Waiting Seats?
Waiting in a queue while standing is difficult or impossible for many PWDs. Designated seating ensures they do not have to choose between holding their place in line and physical exhaustion.

---

## COMPUTATION EXAMPLE: 750-SEAT CINEMA

**Given:** A multiplex cinema has 750 seats in a single auditorium.

**Step 1: Apply 2024 IRR 3% Rule**
$$750 \times 3\% = 22.5 → \textbf{Round up to 23 wheelchair spaces}$$

**Step 2: Apply Old IRR for Comparison**
- 6 spaces for first 500 seats
- Remaining 250 seats above 500: 250 ÷ 100 = 2.5 → 2 additional spaces (or 3, rounding up)
- **Old IRR total: 8 or 9 spaces**

**Step 3: Key Takeaway**
The 2024 rule **dramatically increases** the requirement: 23 vs. 8–9 spaces. This represents a ~2.5× increase in required accessible seating.

**Step 4: Footprint Impact**
- Each space: 900 mm × 1200 mm = 1.08 m²
- 23 spaces: **24.84 m² minimum dedicated to wheelchair seating**
- Plus companion seats, aisle integration, and accessible routes = significant planning impact

**Step 5: Priority Waiting Seats**
- If lobby waiting area has 50 seats: 50 × 5% = **3 priority seats** minimum

```
TIERED CINEMA — PLAN VIEW (Schematic)

SCREEN
|==========================================|
|         GENERAL SEATING (rows A-Z)       |
|                                          |
|  [WC][C]  ← Row L  →  [WC][C]           |
|           ← Row M  →                    |
|  [WC][C]  ← Row R  →  [WC][C]           |
|_________________________________________|
        ↑ Accessible Circulation Route ↑
        (DOES NOT overlap WC spaces above)

[WC] = Wheelchair Space (900×1200mm)
[C]  = Companion Seat (standard seat width)
```

**Key Sightline Rules:**
- WC spaces at **multiple elevations** for unobstructed views
- Spaces **dispersed** across left, center, and right of seating bowl
- Not all grouped in one corner (dispersal requirement implied by "adjoin accessible circulation throughout")

# Legal Liability and Enforcement Workflow


## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the task in one sentence: what concept is being identified, compared, sequenced, or applied? Then anchor your answer to the article's stated scope and avoid importing details from a different topic.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **Legal Liability and Enforcement Workflow** as enough to answer. For exam practice, first identify the exact concept being asked, then choose the option that matches that concept.
### Who Can Sue Whom — The Complete BP 344 / RA 7277 / RA 9442 / RA 10754 Enforcement Chain

---

## REAL-WORLD HOOK

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Explain the Building Official's enforcement workflow — Notice of Violation, Work Stoppage Order, Demolition Order, Administrative Fines — under PD 1096 Rule II; distinguish Light, Less Grave, and Grave violations and their corresponding fines; apply the surcharge calculation for illegal construction; and identify the appeal process for contested orders.
---


A man in a manual wheelchair approaches the entrance of a newly opened three-storey mall in Cebu. There is no ramp. There is no curb cut from the parking lot. The only entrance is up four steps. He photographs everything, calls the NCDA hotline, and files a written complaint with the City Building Official that same afternoon. Within 72 hours, a stop-work order is posted on the building's Certificate of Occupancy — a document the mall paid 18 months to obtain. The architect of record receives a notice from the PRC. The building owner faces a criminal complaint. The structural engineer is left wondering: *how did a four-step entrance cost everyone this much?* This module is your complete map of that enforcement chain — every actor, every remedy, every penalty.

---

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="ra9266", section="Section 29 - Prohibited Acts"
- Text: The enforcement chain: PWD complaint → NCDA/BO investigation → Notice of Violation → Stop Work Order → Fine (up to ₱200,000) → Criminal liability (RA 7277, Sec. 46-47) → PRC revocation for licensed professionals. Every actor in the BOLD-CAPS chain has specific legal responsibilities.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0002 component="ExamTip" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: LEA Pattern: Expect questions testing who bears liability. The Architect of Record bears professional liability under RA 9266. The building Owner bears civil and criminal liability for noncompliance. The Building Official faces administrative liability for failure to enforce.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

## CORE MNEMONIC FRAMEWORK

### "**BOLD-CAPS**" — The Enforcement Actors

| Letter | Actor | Role |
|--------|-------|------|
| **B** | **Building Official (BO)** | Issues/denies permits; primary LGU enforcer |
| **O** | **Owner** | Civilly and criminally liable for noncompliance |
| **L** | **LGU** (Mayor's Office / Sanggunian) | Local legislation; escalation authority |
| **D** | **DPWH** | Promulgates IRR of BP 344; technical authority |
| **C** | **CAAP / Other agencies** | Sector-specific implementing agencies |
| **A** | **Architect of Record** | Professional liability under RA 9266 |
| **P** | **PWD / Organization of PWDs** | Can file complaints at any stage |
| **S** | **NCDA** | Policy coordination; monitoring; formal complaints |

---

## PART I: FULL ENFORCEMENT CHAIN — 20 Q&A FLASHCARDS

---

### CARD 1
**Q: What is the primary legal basis for requiring accessibility features in buildings?**

**A:** Batas Pambansa Blg. 344 (BP 344), enacted in 1983, is the *Accessibility Law* — it mandates that public buildings, institutions, establishments, and public utilities be designed for accessibility by persons with physical handicaps. Its 2024 Revised Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) issued by DPWH provides the specific technical standards. BP 344 is implemented together with:
- **RA 7277** (Magna Carta for Persons with Disability, 1992)
- **RA 9442** (2007 amendment — adds anti-discrimination, expanded discounts)
- **RA 10754** (2016 amendment — 20% discount + VAT exemption)

---

### CARD 2
**Q: Who issues building permits, and how does BP 344 become a condition of the permit?**

**A:** The **Building Official (BO)** — an appointee of the LGU — is the sole authority to issue building permits under PD 1096 (National Building Code). Under BP 344 Sec. 8 and Rule 3 of the IRR:
- The BO **shall not issue** a building permit for covered buildings unless the plans comply with accessibility standards.
- Accessibility compliance is a **mandatory checklist item** during plan review.
- Buildings covered: all public buildings, commercial establishments, hotels, shopping centers, hospitals, schools, transport terminals — essentially all buildings open to the public.
- A plan that fails to show accessible routes, accessible toilets, required ramps, or accessible parking is **legally defective** and must be returned for revision.

---

### CARD 3
**Q: Can a Certificate of Occupancy (COO) be issued for a non-compliant building?**

**A:** **No.** Under BP 344 Rule 3 and PD 1096 Section 309, the BO shall not issue a Certificate of Occupancy unless the completed building conforms to all applicable laws, including BP 344. Specifically:
- An on-site inspection for occupancy must verify that all accessibility features shown in the approved plans are actually installed.
- Missing or substandard features (e.g., ramp too steep, parking not marked, accessible toilet not completed) are grounds to **withhold the COO**.
- If a COO is issued in error, the BO can order cessation of operations until compliance is achieved.

---

### CARD 4
**Q: Who can file a complaint for BP 344 noncompliance, and where?**

**A:** Under BP 344 and RA 7277, the following may file complaints:
1. **Any PWD** — directly to the BO, NCDA, DPWH, or courts
2. **Any organization of PWDs** — same channels
3. **NCDA (National Council on Disability Affairs)** — ex officio monitoring; may file administrative and criminal complaints
4. **DPWH** — as promulgator of the IRR; may conduct inspections and file complaints
5. **Any private citizen** — via BO or courts
6. **Barangay officials** — may endorse complaints to the city/municipal BO

**Where to file:**
- **Step 1:** City/Municipal Building Official (administrative)
- **Step 2:** Regional Office of DPWH (if BO fails to act)
- **Step 3:** NCDA (for policy-level and inter-agency escalation)
- **Step 4:** Regular courts (civil/criminal action)

---

### CARD 5
**Q: What is the role of DPWH in BP 344 enforcement?**

**A:** The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) has three roles:
1. **IRR Promulgation:** DPWH, jointly with DOH, NCDA, and DTI as applicable, issues and updates the IRR of BP 344. The 2024 IRR is the current applicable standard.
2. **Technical Authority:** DPWH provides technical guidance to BOs and resolves interpretation disputes on accessibility standards.
3. **Inspection Authority:** DPWH may conduct independent inspections of covered buildings and file complaints or issue directives to LGUs.

> **Key point:** DPWH does NOT issue building permits — that is the BO/LGU function. DPWH sets the rules; the BO enforces them locally.

---

### CARD 6
**Q: What is the role of NCDA in enforcement?**

**A:** The National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) is the coordinating body for all disability-related policies under RA 7277. In enforcement:
- **Monitoring:** Conducts or coordinates accessibility audits of public buildings
- **Advocacy:** Issues advisories to LGUs, building owners, and agencies
- **Complaints:** May formally lodge complaints with BOs, DPWH, or the Office of the Ombudsman if government buildings are noncompliant
- **Inter-agency coordination:** Works with DOH (health facilities), DepEd/CHED (schools), DOTr (transport) to enforce sector-specific accessibility standards
- **Does NOT issue building permits** or have direct authority to impose fines — it escalates to agencies with that authority

---

### CARD 7
**Q: What criminal penalties apply under BP 344 for noncompliance?**

**A:** Under BP 344 Section 10, as amended by RA 10754:
- **Fine:** ₱5,000 to ₱50,000 (original BP 344 penalty — now effectively superseded by RA 10754 higher penalties for related violations)
- Under **RA 10754 Sec. 32** (amending RA 7277): Any person who violates accessibility provisions may face:
  - **Fine:** Up to **₱300,000**
  - **Imprisonment:** Up to **6 years**
  - Or **both**, at the discretion of the court

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="lea-watch", title="Trap Leart"
- Text: The ₱50,000 fine from original BP 344 is frequently tested as a distractor. The current maximum under RA 10754 is ₱300,000 + 6 years. Always cite the latest amendment.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

### CARD 8
**Q: Under RA 9442, what anti-discrimination provisions have architectural design implications?**

**A:** RA 9442 (amending RA 7277) adds:
- **Sec. 32 (anti-ridicule / anti-discrimination):** Any person who refuses, withholds, or restricts the rights of PWDs — including physical access to public establishments — commits a violation
- **Sec. 33:** Establishments that deny equal physical access (no ramp, no accessible toilet, no accessible parking) may face administrative sanctions AND criminal liability
- **Priority lanes/counters:** Mandatory in all government offices, hospitals, and commercial establishments — these are physical design requirements (counters, queue management, signage) with direct architectural implications
- **Anti-ridicule:** While not a building design standard per se, designing spaces that humiliate PWDs (e.g., making the only accessible toilet a "service toilet" in a back alley) can be cited as a form of discrimination under RA 9442

---

### CARD 9
**Q: What is the architect's professional liability under RA 9266 for accessibility failures?**

**A:** Under the Architecture Act of 2004 (RA 9266):
- An architect bears **professional responsibility** for the design conformity of projects they sign and seal.
- If accessibility features are absent, deficient, or incorrectly designed in the approved plans, the architect of record may face:
  1. **PRC administrative complaint** — suspension or revocation of Professional Identification Card (PIC)
  2. **Civil liability** — RA 9266 Sec. 39 imposes a **10-year civil liability period** for structural and design defects from completion of the project
  3. **Criminal liability** — if the deficiency resulted in injury or death of a PWD (in conjunction with the Revised Penal Code)
- **The 10-year period** means an architect can be sued up to a decade after the building is completed for design failures — including accessibility failures that result in injury.

---

### CARD 10
**Q: Can the building owner be separately liable from the architect?**

**A:** Yes, and often more directly. The building owner has ongoing obligations:
- **Maintenance:** The owner must maintain all accessibility features in working condition at all times. A broken ramp, missing TGSI strips, or padlocked accessible toilet constitute violations even if the original design was compliant.
- **Alteration duty:** Any renovation, alteration, or fit-out must preserve or improve accessibility compliance.
- **Operational liability:** If a PWD is injured because an accessibility feature was absent, defective, or improperly maintained, the owner faces:
  1. Civil damages under the Civil Code (quasi-delict, Art. 2176)
  2. Criminal liability under BP 344 / RA 10754
  3. Administrative action from the BO (suspension of occupancy permit)

> **Key distinction:** The architect's liability is primarily for **design**. The owner's liability is primarily for **construction, maintenance, and operation**. Both can be liable simultaneously.

---

### CARD 11
**Q: What happens if the Building Official issues a permit despite noncompliant plans?**

**A:** The BO is personally liable for administrative and criminal sanctions:
- **Administrative liability:** BO may be charged with dereliction of duty before the Civil Service Commission (CSC) or Office of the Ombudsman
- **Criminal liability:** Under PD 1096 Sec. 213, a BO who issues a permit for a noncompliant building faces imprisonment and/or fine
- **DPWH oversight:** DPWH may investigate the BO and recommend disciplinary action to the Local Chief Executive (Mayor/Governor)
- The permit, if issued improperly, does NOT provide a legal defense to the building owner — the owner remains liable for the underlying noncompliance

---

### CARD 12
**Q: What is the escalation path if the Building Official refuses to act on a complaint?**

**A:** The escalation path is:

```
Level 1 → City/Municipal Building Official
           (initial complaint, inspection request)
              ↓ (no action within 15 days)
Level 2 → DPWH Regional Office
           (technical review; may issue directives to BO)
              ↓ (no action or if government building)
Level 3 → NCDA
           (inter-agency coordination; may escalate to Ombudsman)
              ↓ (criminal violation alleged)
Level 4 → Office of the Ombudsman / Regular Courts
           (criminal complaint; civil action for damages)
              ↓ (professional misconduct alleged)
Level 5 → PRC / PRBoA
           (administrative case against architect)
```

---

### CARD 13
**Q: What are the discounts and VAT exemptions under RA 10754, and who must physically accommodate them?**

**A:** RA 10754 grants PWDs:
- **20% discount** on medicines, medical/dental services, transportation, hotel accommodation, restaurant meals, recreation, and burial services
- **12% VAT exemption** on the same transactions
- **Additional 5% discount** on basic necessities (RA 9442 provision retained)

**Architectural design implications:**
- Pharmacies, hospitals, restaurants, and commercial establishments must have **accessible priority counters** (two-level: 750 mm / 950–1100 mm) where PWDs can transact
- **Express lanes** (with ISA signage) for PWDs at government offices, banks, and commercial establishments
- **Cashier counter design** must accommodate wheelchair approach (700 mm knee clearance under counter, 1500 × 1500 mm approach space)
- The right to the discount is meaningless if the PWD cannot physically reach the counter to claim it — **the discount law is simultaneously an accessibility design mandate**

---

### CARD 14
**Q: Does BP 344 apply to privately owned buildings that are not "public buildings"?**

**A:** BP 344 applies to all **buildings and establishments open to the public** — not just government buildings. Specifically:

| Type of Establishment | BP 344 Applies? |
|----------------------|----------------|
| Government offices | YES |
| Commercial establishments (malls, stores) | YES |
| Hotels and lodging houses (6+ rooms) | YES |
| Hospitals and clinics | YES |
| Schools (public and private) | YES |
| Churches and places of worship | YES |
| Purely private single-family residences | Generally NO (unless requesting for a public business permit) |
| Condominiums (common areas) | YES |
| Private offices (employer) | YES (RA 7277 employment provisions) |

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="Callout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: variant="lea-watch", title="Trap Leart"
- Text: "Private" does not mean "exempt." If the public can enter the building, BP 344 applies.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

### CARD 15
**Q: What is the statute of limitations for filing a criminal complaint under BP 344 / RA 10754?**

**A:** BP 344 violations with penalties of up to 6 years imprisonment fall under the Revised Penal Code's prescriptive periods:
- **Criminal action:** 8 years from discovery of the violation (for offenses punishable by prisión correccional — up to 6 years)
- **Civil action:** 10 years under the Civil Code for written obligations; 4 years for quasi-delicts (from date of injury)
- **Administrative action (PRC):** Subject to PRC's own rules; complaints must generally be filed within a reasonable period from discovery
- **Continuing violations:** A building that remains noncompliant creates a **continuing offense** — the prescriptive period resets each day the violation persists

---

### CARD 16
**Q: What barangay-level role exists in the BP 344 enforcement chain?**

**A:** Barangay officials do not have direct authority to enforce BP 344 or issue building permits. However:
- **Barangay Captains** may receive informal complaints from PWD constituents and refer them to the City/Municipal BO
- **Barangay Health Workers (BHW)** and PWD Affairs Officers may assist PWDs in filing formal complaints
- **Sangguniang Barangay** may pass resolutions urging LGUs to enforce accessibility standards
- Under RA 9442, every LGU (including barangay level) must designate a **PWD Affairs Officer** (PDAO) who serves as a local focal point for accessibility complaints

---

### CARD 17
**Q: What must the architect do when a client instructs them to omit accessibility features to save cost?**

**A:** The architect has a **non-delegable duty** to comply with BP 344:
1. **Inform the client in writing** that BP 344 compliance is mandatory and cannot be waived by either party
2. **Refuse to sign and seal plans** that do not comply with accessibility standards
3. If the client insists, the architect **must withdraw from the project** — continuing to design a noncompliant building exposes the architect to professional and criminal liability
4. The architect's obligation runs to the **public and to PWDs**, not only to the paying client
5. Under RA 9266 Sec. 33, the architect's signature and seal is a **certification of compliance** with all applicable laws — including BP 344

---

### CARD 18
**Q: How does RA 7277 Section 46 interact with BP 344 penalties?**

**A:** RA 7277 Sec. 46 (Penal Clause) provides a general criminal penalty for any violation of the Magna Carta for PWDs, which includes accessibility provisions. RA 10754 (2016) expressly amended and strengthened these penalties:

| Law | Maximum Fine | Maximum Imprisonment |
|-----|-------------|----------------------|
| BP 344 original | ₱50,000 | — (no jail term in original text) |
| RA 7277 Sec. 46 | ₱100,000 | 6 months – 2 years |
| RA 9442 amendment | ₱200,000 | 6 months – 6 years |
| RA 10754 amendment | **₱300,000** | **Up to 6 years** |

> The most recent law (**RA 10754**) controls. Always cite the **₱300,000 fine + 6 years imprisonment** as current maximum.

---

### CARD 19
**Q: What constitutes an accessibility violation that triggers criminal liability (as opposed to a mere administrative violation)?**

**A:** Criminal liability under RA 10754 requires:
1. **Willful non-compliance** — the owner knew of the requirement and failed to comply
2. **Refusal to remedy** — after notice from the BO or DPWH, the owner still did not correct the deficiency
3. **Injury or denial of access** — a PWD was actually denied access or suffered harm due to the missing feature (strengthens the case but not strictly required for criminal filing)

**Administrative violations** (first stage) include:
- Deficient plans submitted for permit
- Minor deviations from approved accessible design during construction
- Failure to maintain features (first notice stage)

**Criminal violations** (escalated stage) include:
- Deliberately omitting accessibility features after BO order
- Padlocking or blocking accessible toilets/routes
- Retaliating against a PWD who complained

---

### CARD 20
**Q: What is the enforcement sequence from plan submission to criminal prosecution?**

**A:**

```
Stage 1 — PLAN REVIEW
  Architect submits plans to BO
  BO checks accessibility compliance (BP 344 checklist)
  Non-compliant → plans returned for revision
  Compliant → Building Permit issued

Stage 2 — CONSTRUCTION INSPECTION
  BO inspects during construction
  Deviations from approved plan → Notice to Correct issued
  Non-compliance → Stop Work Order

Stage 3 — OCCUPANCY INSPECTION
  BO conducts final inspection before issuing COO
  Accessibility features must match approved plans
  Non-compliance → COO withheld
  Continued non-compliance → Referral to LGU legal office

Stage 4 — POST-OCCUPANCY COMPLAINT
  PWD / NCDA / DPWH files complaint
  BO conducts inspection within 15 days
  Violation confirmed → Written Notice of Violation to Owner

Stage 5 — ADMINISTRATIVE ACTION
  BO issues Cease and Desist Order (if continuing violation)
  LGU legal office files administrative case
  BO reports to DPWH Regional Office

Stage 6 — CRIMINAL PROSECUTION
  DPWH or NCDA refers to Office of the City/Provincial Prosecutor
  Prosecutor files Information in court
  Penalties: up to ₱300,000 + 6 years (RA 10754)
  Conviction → civil damages also awarded

Stage 7 — PROFESSIONAL SANCTIONS
  PRC / PRBoA receives referral
  Architect faces suspension or revocation of license
  10-year civil liability period runs from project completion
```

---

## REASON FOR THE LAW

> **Why is the enforcement chain so elaborate?**
>

- Text: The Philippines has approximately 1.57 million registered PWDs (PSA 2020), with the actual number estimated at 3–5 times higher. For decades, accessible design was treated as optional — buildings were approved and occupied with zero accessibility features. The layered enforcement structure (BO → DPWH → NCDA → courts) was designed to create multiple points of accountability. A corrupt or negligent BO is not the end of the road; NCDA and DPWH provide independent oversight, and any PWD can bypass l
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

## TRAP LEARTS (MASTER LIST)

> **🚨 TRAP 1 — Who Promulgates the IRR**
> Exam questions often test "who issues the IRR of BP 344." Answer: **DPWH** (jointly with relevant agencies like DOH, NCDA, DTI). Not PRC, not HLURB/DHSUD, not LGU.

> **🚨 TRAP 2 — Criminal vs Administrative Penalty Amounts**
> ₱50,000 (original BP 344), ₱100,000 (RA 7277), ₱200,000 (RA 9442), **₱300,000** (RA 10754). Always choose the highest = RA 10754.

> **🚨 TRAP 3 — Who Issues the Building Permit**
> The **Building Official** (LGU appointee) issues building permits — not DPWH, not NCDA, not PRC. DPWH sets the rules; the BO applies them.

> **🚨 TRAP 4 — Architect's Civil Liability Period**
> RA 9266 gives a **10-year civil liability period** for design defects from project completion — NOT the general 4-year quasi-delict period or 3-year criminal prescriptive period. The 10-year period is specific to RA 9266.

> **🚨 TRAP 5 — NCDA Cannot Issue Building Permits or Impose Fines**
> NCDA is a **coordinating and monitoring body**. It cannot issue permits, impose fines, or order building closures directly. It must refer to the BO, DPWH, or courts to enforce.

---

## ACTIVE RECALL DRILL

**Q1.** Who promulgates the IRR of BP 344?
> **A: DPWH** (jointly with DOH, NCDA, DTI as applicable).

**Q2.** What is the maximum criminal penalty under RA 10754?
> **A: ₱300,000 fine + 6 years imprisonment**, or both.

**Q3.** Can the Building Official be held liable for issuing a permit for a noncompliant building?
[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]

- Text: A: Yes — administrative (CSC/Ombudsman) and criminal (PD 1096 Sec. 213) liability.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Q4.** What is the architect's civil liability period under RA 9266?
> **A: 10 years** from completion of the project.

**Q5.** Name three parties who can file a BP 344 complaint.
> **A:** Any PWD, any organization of PWDs, NCDA, DPWH, any private citizen.

---

## PROTÉGÉ EFFECT CHALLENGE

> **Your task:** A newly licensed architect tells you: "My client owns the building; if there's a penalty, it's the owner's problem, not mine."
>
> Correct this misconception using only the content of this module. Address:
> 1. The architect's personal criminal exposure under RA 10754
> 2. The civil liability period under RA 9266
> 3. The PRC administrative consequences
> 4. The architect's duty when a client asks to omit accessibility features
> 5. Why signing and sealing a noncompliant plan is the specific act that creates liability
>
> If you can deliver this correction fluently, you have internalized the enforcement framework.

---

## Board Exam Quick Check

Before memorizing details from this topic, state the task in one sentence: what concept is being identified, compared, sequenced, or applied? Then anchor your answer to the article's stated scope and avoid importing details from a different topic.

**Common mistake:** treating a familiar keyword in **Interior Doors and Hardware** as enough to answer. For exam practice, first identify the exact concept being asked, then choose the option that matches that concept.
### BP 344 (2024 IRR) — Philippine Architecture Licensure Exam Review

---

## REAL-WORLD HOOK

You are a wheelchair user arriving at a mall's cinema restroom. The door looks wide enough — but you press the lever handle and it swings *toward* you. There is no kick plate, the threshold catches your front caster wheel, and the vision panel is a narrow slit that no one can see through. You cannot tell if someone is on the other side, and you cannot push against it with your chair. Every measurement in this module exists because that experience is a failure of architecture.

---

| **Weight-activated door minimum trigger** | **10 lbs / ~4.5 kg** | App. A, General Provisions | Must respond to service animals |
| **Lever handles (lodging)** | Required in accessible guest rooms | Sec. 17.1 | Operable with closed fist |
| **Door swing — general** | Swing away from accessible path | App. A, General Provisions | Do not swing into accessible clear floor space |

---

## SPATIAL SKETCH — HOW TO MEASURE 900 mm CLEAR WIDTH

```
   JAMB                              JAMB
     |                                |
     |<---------- 900 mm ----------->|
     |   (measured face-to-face       |
     |    with door leaf at 90°)      |
     |                                |
 ====[DOOR LEAF]========================
                    ↑
         Door leaf swings to 90°;
         measure the FREE PASSAGE,
         not the nominal door size.
```

> **Why this matters on exams:** A 900 mm door leaf in a standard 100 mm jamb does NOT give 900 mm clear. The leaf itself takes up ~35–45 mm. Always measure the clear passage, not the door leaf dimension.

---

## > TRAP LEART #1 — The "900 mm Nominal" Trick

**Question stem:** *"A single-leaf door has a 900 mm leaf width. Is this compliant with BP 344?"*

**Wrong answer:** Yes — 900 mm is the minimum.

**Correct answer:** **It depends.** The 900 mm requirement is for **clear width**, measured face-of-door-at-90°-to-jamb. A 900 mm leaf in a standard frame typically yields only ~855–870 mm clear. A **950–965 mm leaf** is usually needed to achieve 900 mm clear passage.

---

## > TRAP LEART #2 — Single vs. Double Leaf

**Question stem:** *"A pair of fire exit doors has two 900 mm leaves. What is the minimum required clear width under BP 344?"*

**Wrong answer:** 900 mm (one leaf is enough).

**Correct answer:** Double-leaf doors require **1,800 mm** combined clear width (App. A). Both leaves are measured together. Each leaf must contribute.

---

## > TRAP LEART #3 — Threshold Height Confusion

**Question stem:** *"A threshold is 8 mm high with a beveled profile. Is this compliant?"*

**Correct answer:** **Yes.** Beveling is required for thresholds **between 6 mm and 12 mm**. At 8 mm, the threshold must be beveled — and it is. However, a flat (unbeveled) 8 mm threshold would be non-compliant.

**The rule:** ≤6 mm → flush acceptable. 6–12 mm → **must bevel**. >12 mm → **not permitted**.

---

## > TRAP LEART #4 — Vision Panel vs. Sidelight

The **100 mm** minimum refers to the **vision panel width** (the glazed window in the door leaf). Do not confuse with a full-height sidelight panel beside the door. They serve different purposes. The vision panel lets approaching persons see each other before the door swings open.

---

## > TRAP LEART #5 — Dressing Room Door Swing

**Question stem:** *"Which direction must accessible dressing room doors swing?"*

**Correct answer:** **Outward.** This is a safety requirement, not just an accessibility one. If a person with a disability collapses inside, the outward swing allows rescuers to open the door without the body blocking it.

---

## REASON FOR THE LAW

| Rule | Why It Exists |
|------|--------------|
| **900 mm clear width** | Minimum for a manual wheelchair (typical width ~680 mm) plus 110 mm each side for hand clearance during propulsion |
| **Lever handles at 900 mm** | Operable with a closed fist, elbow, or forearm — usable by persons with no hand grip. Height matches seated reach envelope (850–1,000 mm AFF) |
| **Kick plate 300–400 mm** | Protects door from footrests and wheelchair footplates. Without it, doors degrade quickly in high-traffic accessible routes |
| **Threshold max 12 mm / bevel if >6 mm** | Front caster wheels of wheelchairs (typically 75–150 mm diameter) can catch on abrupt transitions >6 mm, causing tipping |
| **Vision panel min 100 mm** | A person in a wheelchair sits lower (~1.1–1.3 m eye level). A narrow panel must still be visible from seated height |
| **Frameless glass markings 900–1,500 mm AFF** | Persons with low vision may not see clear glass. The marking band crosses the seated *and* standing field of view |
| **Dressing rooms open outward** | Emergency egress principle: if user falls against door, door must still be openable. Also prevents door from striking a person transferring to/from a wheelchair |
| **Sensory room: no threshold, easy to open** | Persons with autism, anxiety, or sensory processing differences may panic at barriers. Easy egress = safety + dignity |
| **Automatic doors at transport facilities** | Heavy commuter bags, strollers, crutches, and high passenger volume make manual doors a bottleneck and hazard |

---

## DOOR HARDWARE DECISION TREE

```
Is the door on a major circulation route?
├── YES → Kick plate required (300–400 mm)
│         Handle: lever or vertical pull at 900 mm
│         Vision panel: min 100 mm wide
│         Threshold: max 12 mm, bevel if 6–12 mm
│         Consider: automatic door (transport fac.)
│
└── NO  → Still needs 900 mm clear, lever handle,
          threshold rules still apply
          Kick plate: recommended but check context

Is it a glass door (frameless, full-height)?
└── YES → High-contrast marking band: 900–1,500 mm AFF

Is it a dressing room door?
└── YES → Must swing OUTWARD

Is it a sensory room door?
└── YES → No threshold; easy-to-open hardware

Is it a lodging/guest room?
└── YES → Lever handle required (Sec. 17.1)
          Secondary peephole at 1,000 mm AFF
```

---

## LOBBY DOORS vs. FIRE EXIT DOORS — COMPARISON TABLE

| Feature | Lobby / Interior Door | Fire Exit Door |
|--------|----------------------|---------------|
| Min clear width | 900 mm | 900 mm (same) |
| Hardware | Lever handle preferred | Panic bar (push-to-open) preferred |
| Closing speed | Not specified for accessibility alone | Must allow safe egress |
| Automatic option | Preferred at transport facilities | Must also be manual-operable during power failure |
| Kick plate | 300–400 mm on major routes | Strongly recommended |
| Vision panel | 100 mm min width | 100 mm min width (BP 344) |
| Opening force | As low as possible; no specific value in BP 344 for standard doors | Governed by fire code — but accessibility requires low force |
| Threshold | Max 12 mm, bevel if >6 mm | Same; fire-rated thresholds must still comply |

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="bp344", title="the stricter clear width governs."
- Text: Cross-reference: PD 1096 (National Building Code) governs fire exit door widths and panic hardware. BP 344 governs the accessibility dimension of those same doors. Both apply simultaneously — the stricter clear width governs.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

## ACTIVE RECALL DRILL

**Q1.** What is the minimum clear width for a single-leaf accessible door under BP 344 2024 IRR?
> **A1.** 900 mm, measured face of door at 90° to jamb.

**Q2.** At what height is the standard handle/pull/latch required to be centered?
> **A2.** 900 mm above finished floor (AFF).

**Q3.** A threshold is 10 mm high. What must be done to make it compliant?
> **A3.** It must be beveled. (Beveling is required for thresholds between 6 mm and 12 mm.)

**Q4.** What is the minimum width of a vision panel in a door leaf?
> **A4.** 100 mm.

**Q5.** At what heights must markings appear on a frameless full-height glass door?
> **A5.** Between 900 mm and 1,500 mm AFF (a marking band spanning this zone).

**Q6.** Which direction must accessible dressing room doors swing, and why?
> **A6.** Outward — so that if a person collapses inside, the door can still be opened by rescuers.

**Q7.** What is the maximum threshold height allowed under BP 344?
> **A7.** 12 mm (and must be beveled if between 6 mm and 12 mm).

**Q8.** Where are kick plates required, and what is the height range?
> **A8.** On major circulation route doors; kick plate height: 300–400 mm.

**Q9.** What are the dimensions for a double-leaf accessible door?
> **A9.** Minimum 1,800 mm combined clear width.

**Q10.** At what height is the secondary peephole installed for wheelchair users?
> **A10.** 1,000 mm AFF (in addition to the standard-height peephole).

---

## 60-SECOND BLITZ QUIZ

*Answer in 6 seconds each — go!*

1. Min clear width, single door → **900 mm**
2. Min clear width, double-leaf → **1,800 mm**
3. Handle height → **900 mm AFF**
4. Max threshold height → **12 mm**
5. Bevel required above → **6 mm**
6. Vision panel min width → **100 mm**
7. Kick plate height range → **300–400 mm**
8. Glass door marking zone → **900–1,500 mm AFF**
9. Dressing room door swings → **Outward**
10. Secondary peephole height → **1,000 mm AFF**

**Score: 10/10? You own this topic.**

---

## PROTÉGÉ EFFECT CHALLENGE

You are teaching a first-year architecture student who just drew a restroom door at 850 mm clear width with a round knob at 1,050 mm and a 15 mm flat threshold. Without looking at your notes, explain to them:

1. **Why each of the three elements is non-compliant** (cite the specific BP 344 provision for each).
2. **What the corrected drawing must show** (exact dimensions).
3. **Why these rules matter in real life** — tell the story of the wheelchair user who could not enter.

*If you can explain it to a student, you have internalized it for the exam.*

---

*Next: Module 6 — Fixtures & Small Items in Common Areas*
*Previous: Module 4 — Assembly Seating & Waiting Areas*

[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

## Exam Tip

ALE Trap: Minimum clear opening width = 900 mm for accessible doors, 700 mm for interior non-accessible. Fire doors must be self-closing with positive latching. Panic hardware required on exit doors of Group E, F, H, I occupancies. The clear opening is measured with door at 90° — NOT the door leaf width.

## Reciprocity Principles in Architectural Practice (RA 9266 Section 27)

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Define reciprocity principles in architectural licensing.
- Explain how reciprocity applies to foreign architects seeking Philippine registration.
- Identify countries with which the Philippines has reciprocity agreements.
- Distinguish reciprocity from the ASEAN MRA.

---

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0001 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="ra9266", section="Section 24 - Reciprocity"
- Text: Expect 1-2 reciprocity questions per exam cycle. The most common trap: conflating Section 27 and Section 38. Know which is which cold.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

### The Reciprocity Requirement

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0002 component="LawCallout" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: code="irr", section="RA 9266, Section 27"
- Text: A person who is not a citizen of the Philippines at the time of applying to take the licensure examination shall not be allowed to take the exam unless proof exists that the foreign country either (a) admits Filipino citizens to practice architecture without restriction, or (b) allows them to practice after an examination on terms of strict and absolute equality with its own citizens, including unconditional recognition of prerequisite degrees from Philippine institutions.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0003 component="Warn" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: The previous version of this article claimed a foreign applicant could prove "reciprocity OR substantial equivalence in education, training, and experience." This is incorrect. The phrase "substantial equivalence" does NOT appear in RA 9266 Section 27. The only pathway under the law is **proof of reciprocal treatment** by the foreign country.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

Reciprocity exists when a foreign country admits Filipino architects to practice without restriction, or allows them to take an examination on fully equal terms. "Strict and absolute equality" means:
- Equal examination conditions (same test, same language, same fees)
- Unconditional recognition of Philippine architecture degrees
- No hidden barriers (additional training, extra fees, or evaluation procedures)

The foreign country's law must specifically provide for this — not merely allow it in practice.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0004 component="Note" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: **Why "law, not practice" matters.** If a foreign country merely tolerates Filipino architects working there without a written statutory right, that does not satisfy Section 27. The applicant must point to a specific legal provision in the foreign jurisdiction that grants Filipino architects equal access. This is a common exam trap: an answer choice describing a country's "established practice" of admitting Filipino architects sounds correct but fails because the law does not explicitly provide 
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

### Section 27 vs Section 38: Two Separate Pathways

This is the most commonly tested distinction on the topic.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0005 component="Tip" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: Think of these as two different doors: Section 27 leads to **full Philippine licensure** (you pass the exam, you become a licensed Philippine architect). Section 38 leads to a **temporary permit** for a specific project (you remain licensed in your home country, you work on one project with a Filipino counterpart). You go through one door or the other — not both.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

| Pathway | Legal Basis | What It Grants | Requirements |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full licensure via exam | Section 27 | Philippine architect license (permanent, renewable) | Prove reciprocity, pass the LEA, meet all registration requirements |
| Temporary/special permit | Section 38 | Project-specific practice permit (temporary, with Filipino counterpart) | Foreign national, specific project, Filipino counterpart, Board approval |

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0006 component="Warn" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: The previous version of this article claimed that "all foreign architects, including those from reciprocal countries, must secure a temporary/special permit under Section 38." This is incorrect. A foreign national who passes the Philippine exam under Section 27 becomes a **licensed Philippine architect** and does NOT need a Section 38 permit.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

**Section 27 pathway:** A foreign national from a reciprocal country applies to take the LEA. If they prove reciprocity, pass the exam, and meet all requirements, they become a registered and licensed Philippine architect. They practice under the same rules as any Filipino architect.

**Section 38 pathway:** A foreign national who is licensed in their home country (but not in the Philippines) can obtain a temporary or special permit to provide architectural services on a specific project. This permit is project-specific, requires a Filipino counterpart architect, and is granted at the Board's discretion. It applies to both reciprocal and non-reciprocal country nationals.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0007 component="Tip" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: **Exam shortcut.** When reading a fact pattern about a foreign architect in the Philippines, ask: *\"Are they taking the Philippine exam?\"* If yes → Section 27 (reciprocity needed, leads to full license). If no → Section 38 (temporary permit, Filipino counterpart required, Board approval). This single question resolves most pathway-distinction items on the LEA.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

### How Reciprocity Is Assessed

The Board of Architecture evaluates whether a foreign country actually grants reciprocity to Filipino architects. This assessment may be based on:
- The foreign country's laws and regulations
- Embassy certifications or foreign board confirmations
- Evidence submitted by the applicant

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0008 component="Warn" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: The article previously claimed the Board "maintains a list of countries with which reciprocity exists." The Board evaluates reciprocity evidence on a case-by-case or ad hoc basis. There is no widely published standing list comparable to those in other professions. The phrasing "the Board maintains a list" overstates the formalization of this process.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

If a country withdraws reciprocal rights, the Board restricts access for that country's nationals. If new reciprocity is established, the Board certifies it and opens examination access.

---

### What the Exam Tests

LEA questions on this topic typically test three things:

| Type | Example |
|------|---------|
| **Definition** | "What does 'strict and absolute equality' require under Section 27?" |
| **Pathway distinction** | "Does a foreign architect from a reciprocal country need a Section 38 permit?" |
| **Scope of reciprocity** | "What must a foreign applicant prove before taking the Philippine exam?" |

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0009 component="ExamTip" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: **Exam strategy.** Reciprocity questions on the LEA usually follow one pattern: a fact scenario describing a foreign architect's situation, then a question about what they need or which section applies. The distractors often mix up Section 27 and Section 38 requirements. Write a quick 2-column table on scratch paper before reading the answer choices — one column for Section 27 (full license via exam, needs reciprocity proof, no counterpart required after passing) and one for Section 38 (temporar
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

### Common Misunderstandings

- **"Substantial equivalence" is NOT in RA 9266 Section 27.** The law requires proof of reciprocity — not an alternative "substantial equivalence" pathway. This error appears in some older review materials.
- **Section 27 and Section 38 are alternatives, not sequential.** Passing the exam under Section 27 means you are a licensed Philippine architect. You do not also need a Section 38 permit.
- **"All foreign architects need a temporary permit" is wrong.** Only those who have NOT passed the Philippine exam need a Section 38 permit. Those who pass the exam practice like any other licensed architect.
- **The Board does not maintain a published reciprocity list.** Reciprocity is evaluated case by case based on evidence.

[SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK:ui_0010 component="Warn" status="preserved"]
Extracted summary:
- Props: (none)
- Text: **High-risk trap.** Of all the corrected errors in this article, the "substantial equivalence" myth is the most dangerous on exam day. Some older review materials and online forums still parrot this incorrect doctrine. If you see "substantial equivalence in education, training, and experience" as an answer choice for Section 27 requirements, eliminate it immediately — the law requires actual proof of reciprocity, nothing less.
[/SLATECAMP_UI_BLOCK]

---

### Practice

**Recall:**
What two things must a foreign country provide for Section 27 reciprocity to exist?

**Apply:**
A foreign architect from Singapore wants to practice in the Philippines on a single hotel project for 6 months. They do not plan to take the Philippine exam. Which section applies, and what requirements must they meet?

**Transfer:**
A foreign architect from a reciprocal country passes the Philippine LEA and registers as a licensed architect. Their client later asks if they need a Filipino counterpart under Section 38. What do you tell them, and why?

## Comprehensive Architectural Services: The Full-Spectrum Commission

## Learning Goal

After studying this article, you should be able to:

- Define comprehensive architectural services (full-spectrum commission).
- Describe all phases from pre-design through post-construction under one contract.
- Explain the advantages of a comprehensive contract for the client and architect.

|---
### Understanding Comprehensive Services

Comprehensive Architectural Services encompasses five primary categories: pre-design services, regular design services, specialized architectural services, construction services, and post-construction services. The architect functions as the _prime professional_, serving as the client's agent in coordinating all necessary services for project delivery. This coordinating role defines the architect's leadership position within the project team.

The architect is shown as prime professional coordinating all categories.", suggestedAsset="Diagram or reference image", status="placeholder"

The architect is not expected to perform all services directly.

### The Five Service Categories

_Pre-design services_ establish the project foundation through consultation, feasibility studies, site analysis, and architectural programming. These services determine the project's viability and establish performance requirements.

_Regular design services_ include the five traditional project phases: Project Definition, Schematic Design, Design Development, Contract Documents, and Bidding or Negotiation. This work creates the design that becomes the basis for construction.

_Specialized architectural services_ expand the core offering to include acoustic design, architectural interiors, site development planning, heritage conservation, security evaluation, facilities maintenance support, and building testing. These services address specific project needs.

_Construction services_ encompass fulltime supervision and construction management, ensuring the architect's design is properly executed in the field.

_Post-construction services_ include building administration and post-construction evaluation, allowing the architect to assess how the completed building performs.

### The Architect's Coordinating Role

In comprehensive services, the architect assumes professional responsibility and civil liability for both design and construction aspects of the project. The architect's education, training, and expertise qualify the professional to take a direct role from conceptualization through implementation.

This extended engagement creates continuity of service, which is essential for executing a completely viable project. The architect coordinates structural engineers, mechanical engineers, landscape architects, specialty consultants, and construction personnel. This coordination ensures seamless integration of all project elements.

When the client hires an architect to coordinate the complete range of Comprehensive Architectural Services, this relationship constitutes _Project Management (PM)_. Project Management represents the owner's engagement of the architect for the full scope of professional responsibility.
